cues.observation: Green street blade reading 'Calle 10' with a one-way arrow — the Calle/Carrera grid naming system is characteristic of Colombia.

Spanish commercial text 'Red de servicios farmacéuticos', 'SAS' (Sociedad por Acciones Simplificada, a Colombian corporate suffix), prices as '$21.999' with dot thousands separator typical of Colombian peso pricing.
Pharmacy chain banner 'Sikuany SAS' with a branch label ('Sede ... Cumaral'); 'Sikuani' is the name of a Llanos indigenous people, tying the brand to the Orinoquía region.
Single-storey painted masonry houses with corrugated zinc/fibre-cement roofs, barred windows, no glazing needs — hot lowland construction rather than Andean brick two-storey with steep tile roofs.

Wide tree-planted central median boulevard with painted kerbs, concrete slab pavement and low traffic — typical planned grid of a small Meta/Casanare llanos town.
Small-displacement commuter motorcycles dominate over cars, parked at kerb; heavy motorcycle dependence is standard in Colombian provincial towns.
Flat street grid but a low green ridge visible on the far right horizon — consistent with the Andean foothills edge (piedemonte llanero) rather than the fully flat deep llanos.

analysis.cultural_economic_read: A small, low-income but tidy provincial town in the Colombian Eastern Plains piedmont: one-storey painted masonry homes, informal street-front eateries with plastic chairs, motorcycle-based mobility, and a regional pharmacy chain rather than national supermarkets. Economy is agropastoral (cattle, rice, oil palm) with services oriented toward nearby Villavicencio. Cultural sphere is mestizo llanero (Hispanic criollo with indigenous Sikuani naming legacy), not Andean highland nor Caribbean coastal.

Presence of a regional pharmacy chain with a branded branch and air conditioning indicates formal retail penetration; overall lower-middle-income, agriculture/cattle-service economy of the Meta piedmont, within Bogotá's commercial orbit via the Villavicencio corridor.

correction.summary: HIT: Colombia / Meta / Cumaral confirmed to within 0.24 km. The decisive chain was the Spanish "SAS" legal suffix plus peso-magnitude pricing ($21.999 with dot thousands separator), the green "Calle 10" blade of the Colombian Calle/Carrera grid, and the pharmacy banner's own branch label reading "Cumaral" together with the Llanos-associated "Sikuany" brand. Venezuela and Ecuador were correctly excluded on currency magnitude, legal-form suffix and street-signage style; the Andean/Caribbean alternatives were excluded by lowland zinc-roof, whitewashed-trunk, wide concrete-slab street typology.

discriminators.title: SAS suffix marks Colombia, not Venezuela or Ecuador
discriminators.body: In Colombia small and mid-sized firms almost universally carry the 'SAS' (Sociedad por Acciones Simplificada) suffix on shopfront signage. In Venezuela you would instead see 'C.A.' or 'S.A.', and in Ecuador 'Cía. Ltda.' or 'S.A.'; Peru uses 'S.A.C.'. A painted or printed 'SAS' after a brand name is one of the fastest single-word country locks in Latin America.

discriminators.title: Green Calle/Carrera blades vs other Latin street signage
discriminators.body: Colombian towns sign their orthogonal grid with small green blades reading 'Calle N' or 'Carrera N', frequently paired with a separate blue one-way arrow plate. In Venezuela and Ecuador you would instead see named streets on white or blue plates, and Ecuadorian towns commonly use larger blue-and-white municipal signs with a coat of arms. Numeric Calle/Carrera pairing is near-diagnostic of Colombia.

discriminators.title: Llanos piedmont town fabric vs Amazonian frontier town
discriminators.body: Meta/Casanare piedmont towns show fully paved concrete-slab streets with planted medians, whitewashed tree trunks, trimmed mango and ceiba canopy and painted masonry houses under zinc. In an Amazonian frontier town (Caquetá, Putumayo, Amazonas) you would instead see more unpaved or mud-stained streets, denser continuous rainforest canopy at the town edge, more timber construction and no dry-season leafless trees. Seasonal deciduous trees standing next to evergreen ones is a savanna marker.

discriminators.title: Peso magnitude with dot separators rules out dollarized Ecuador
discriminators.body: Colombian retail prices run to four or five digits with a dot as thousands separator and no cents, e.g. '$21.999'. In Ecuador (and Panama/El Salvador) you would instead see two-decimal USD prices like '$4.99', and in Peru an 'S/' prefix. Price magnitude alone separates the peso countries from the dollarized ones.

discriminators.title: Indigenous brand names hint at macro-region inside Colombia
discriminators.body: Commercial brands built on Sikuani/Guahibo or llanero imagery cluster in the Orinoquía (Meta, Casanare, Vichada, Arauca). In Andean Colombia you would instead find Muisca/Chibcha or coffee-culture references, and on the Caribbean coast Wayuu or vallenato motifs. Reading the ethnic reference in a chain's name is a legitimate regional narrower once the country is fixed.
